title: Did Jesus Really Rise from the Dead?
excerpt: The four strongest alternatives to the resurrection are theft, the wrong tomb, visions and legend, and every one of them first appears in the New Testament itself. Each explains something. What history can do with them, and where it has to stop, is narrower than either side usually admits.
body:
A history teacher can believe in God on a good day. What he cannot believe is that a man who had been dead since Friday afternoon walked out of a tomb on Sunday morning. A woman who has sung the Easter hymns for forty years found this spring that she could no longer say whether she thinks it happened or only loves the song. A college freshman has been handed a printed list of proofs by a campus group, and something about the list bothers him. It is too tidy, and nobody he respects argues that way about anything else.

Nothing here will prove the resurrection to any of them. Another essay on this site, on [whether the resurrection happened](/writing/did-the-resurrection-happen), lays out the case that it did. This one gives the floor to the other side. It takes the four strongest alternatives, each as its own defenders put it, and asks what each explains and what each still has to explain. Then it says what historical evidence can settle and where it stops.

## The Doubts Are in the Book

A reader who opens the Gospels expecting pious certainty finds something else. Every explanation a skeptic has ever proposed is already there, usually in the mouth of a disciple.

When the women returned with their report, the apostles heard it the way the history teacher does: "these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them" (Luke 24:11). Mary Magdalene's own first explanation was that someone had moved the body. "They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him" (John 20:2). She asked a man she took for the gardener where he had put it. When the disciples saw Jesus, they reached for the category their world already had, and "thought they saw a spirit" (Luke 24:37). Thomas said that unless he could put his hand into the wounds, "I will never believe" (John 20:25). Matthew records the story the guards were paid to tell: "His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep" (Matthew 28:13).

So the theories of mistake, of a ghost and of theft were not invented by the Enlightenment. They were the first things the first witnesses thought. A century and a half later the pagan critic Celsus, whose book survives in the reply Origen wrote to it, ran through the Greek stories of heroes who came back from the underworld, called them myths, and put the issue as well as anyone has: "the question is, whether any one who was really dead ever rose with a veritable body."

## Theft

The oldest alternative is that the body was removed by Jesus' own followers, who then proclaimed a miracle. Matthew answers it in his last chapter. In the middle of the second century the Christian writer Justin still knew the charge in almost the same words, that "his disciples stole him by night from the tomb." About 200 Tertullian mocked it, along with a rival version in which "the gardener abstracted" the body so that visitors would not trample his lettuces. In the 1770s the German scholar Hermann Samuel Reimarus gave it its modern form.

Its strength is its plainness. It asks for nothing unusual, and it accounts for an empty tomb with a single ordinary act. Religious frauds have happened, and the disciples had a motive. They had left their work and their families for a man who was then executed as a criminal, and the alternative to a miracle was to go home as fools.

What it has to explain is everything that came after the tomb. Theft produces a missing body. It does not produce the conviction of people outside the circle, and two of the earliest names on the list were outside it. Paul describes himself as a man who "persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it" (Galatians 1:13). Of Jesus' own family John says, "not even his brothers believed in him" (John 7:5), and yet his brother James appears in Paul's list of witnesses and later headed the Jerusalem church. The theory also has to explain the conduct of the thieves. One of them, James the brother of John, was killed "with the sword" (Acts 12:2), and the others spent their lives saying a thing they knew to be false. That people die for a belief shows nothing about whether it is true. It does show that they hold it, and men who had hidden the body would have known better. Few scholars of any persuasion defend the theft theory now.

## The Wrong Tomb

The second alternative needs no liar at all, only a mistake. In 1907 the New Testament scholar Kirsopp Lake proposed that the women, who were visitors to Jerusalem, came in the half-light to the wrong grave. A young man standing nearby tried to help. "He is not here," he said, and pointed: "See the place where they laid him" (Mark 16:6). The women misunderstood, panicked and ran. On this reading the words "He has risen" were supplied later, by people who already believed.

There are older and harsher versions of the same idea. One is Mary's own guess, that somebody moved the body, and Tertullian's joke about the gardener shows it was in circulation by his day. Another is that there was never a known tomb to find. Rome often left the crucified unburied or put them in a common grave, and the site's page on [the empty tomb](/questions/jesus/the-empty-tomb) calls this "the most disputed part of the historical case."

The strength of this family of theories is that it fits how people behave. John says it was "still dark" (John 20:1). The women had watched an execution two days before. One rock-cut grave looks much like another, and nobody in the story was expecting anything except a corpse.

Its difficulties are of a practical kind. Mark notes, as if he saw the objection coming, that two of the women "saw where he was laid" (Mark 15:47). The man who buried him was known, a member of the council, and could have settled the matter in an afternoon. And as far as the surviving sources show, the first opponents of the church never said the body was still in its grave. They said it had been stolen, which assumes that the right tomb was known to be empty. A defender of the theory can reply that Mark's note is exactly the kind of detail a later writer adds, and that silence from opponents proves little. That is fair. But the theory has a deeper limit. An empty grave convinced nobody. It made Mary think of grave robbers. The wrong tomb, if it happened, accounts for the first hour of Easter and nothing after it.

## Visions

The third alternative is the strongest, and it is the one Celsus thought of: the witnesses dreamed, or saw what they longed to see. Its modern defenders make a careful case, as the site's page on [the appearances and the alternatives](/questions/jesus/the-appearances-and-the-alternatives) sets out. The German scholar Gerd Lüdemann argued in 1994 that Peter's vision came out of grief and guilt after he denied his master, that Paul's came out of a buried unease about his own campaign against the church, and that the appearances to groups spread among excited followers. The theory has data behind it. In 1971 a doctor in Wales interviewed 293 widows and widowers and found that nearly half of them had had some experience of the husband or wife they had lost, often a felt presence, sometimes a sight or a voice.

This should be granted in full. Such experiences are real, common and no sign of madness. The disciples were bereaved, frightened and ashamed, which is the condition in which they occur. A Christian who waves this theory away has not understood how many sane people have seen their dead.

What it has to explain begins with the two outsiders again. Paul was not mourning Jesus, and James, as far as the Gospels say, had not believed in him. It has to explain the appearances to groups, including the one Paul numbers at "more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive" (1 Corinthians 15:6). It needs the tomb to have been lost or left unchecked. And it has to explain the word. The disciples knew what a vision of a dead man was, and Luke says a spirit was their first thought. What they went on to announce was something their world had another word for, a body raised, which nobody expected to happen to one man in the middle of history.

The honest limit runs in both directions. No one can show that Paul had no hidden turmoil, and no one can show that he had. A guess about a mind two thousand years gone is still a guess, whichever side makes it.

## Legend

The fourth alternative does not explain the first Easter. It explains the stories. Set the Gospels in the order most scholars date them, and the appearances grow. Mark is the earliest, and its oldest copies stop with frightened women leaving the tomb. The risen Jesus never comes on stage. Matthew has a short meeting and a mountain. In Luke the risen Jesus walks a road, invites touch and eats: "They gave him a piece of broiled fish, and he took it and ate before them" (Luke 24:42–43). In John he offers his wounds to Thomas. A gospel from the second century goes much further. On this view the earliest Christians believed that God had exalted Jesus to heaven and shown him to them in splendor, and the flesh and the fish came afterward, over decades, as an answer to doubters.

There is truth here that Christians should not dodge. The later accounts are fuller, and the four do not agree in their details, a problem with [a page of its own](/questions/jesus/the-resurrection-accounts-disagree) on this site.

What the theory has to explain is the oldest evidence, which is earlier than any Gospel. Paul wrote to Corinth in the 50s and quoted a summary he says he had himself been given: "that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve" (1 Corinthians 15:4–5). The usual scholarly judgment, shared by many who are not Christians, is that this summary was already fixed a few years after Jesus died. Paul had not picked it up from rumor. By his own account he had spent fifteen days with Cephas in Jerusalem and had met "James the Lord's brother" (Galatians 1:19). Legends need time and distance, and the claim itself had neither. A defender can answer that Paul's list speaks only of appearances and says nothing of a body that ate fish. That point stands. The details of the telling may have grown, but the claim that he was raised and seen was there at the start.

## All Four Together

The best form of the case against uses none of these alone. It takes a little from each. Perhaps the body was never in a private tomb, and within weeks nobody could have said where it lay. Peter, sick with guilt, saw his master. His certainty spread through a frightened group, as certainty does. Paul had a crisis of his own on a road. James came around when his brother's movement grew, and the touchable body arrived later in the telling.

Each piece of that is possible, and a Christian who says otherwise is bluffing. The trouble is that the pieces multiply, and each is thinnest where it carries the most weight. But the real force of the combined theory was never in its details. It lies in a principle: any chain of natural events, however unlikely, is more probable than a dead man rising. Everything turns on whether that principle is true.

## What History Can and Cannot Do

Historians of every persuasion grant more than the popular arguments on either side suggest. Jesus was crucified under Pontius Pilate. Soon afterward some of his followers were convinced they had seen him alive, and so was a man who had been trying to destroy them. The scholar E. P. Sanders, who was no defender of the faith, wrote as the site's page quotes him: "That Jesus' followers (and later Paul) had resurrection experiences is, in my judgement, a fact. What the reality was that gave rise to the experiences I do not know."

His second sentence matters as much as his first. Historians do not agree about the empty tomb. They do not agree about what the experiences were. That God raised Jesus is not a finding of historical scholarship, and it could not be one.

History works by probability, and it measures probability by what usually happens. The dead usually stay dead. The disciples knew that as well as anyone, which is why they called the first report an idle tale. A method built on the usual has no instrument for the unique, and none for the acts of God. It can establish that a man was executed, that a claim was made early, in the very city where the grave was, by named people who paid for it. Paul could tell a Roman governor that "this has not been done in a corner" (Acts 26:26). All of that is public and leaves traces.

The last step is beyond its reach. Whether "God raised him" is the best account of those traces turns on an earlier question, which is whether a God exists who could and would. History neither proves that nor rules it out. A rule that no miracle may ever be concluded is a starting point a person brings to the evidence. It is not something the evidence taught him. The same is true of the believer's readiness to accept one. Both the history teacher and the woman with the hymnbook come to the tomb already carrying something.

We have not always been honest about this. The freshman's list is our doing. We have told people the resurrection is proved beyond reasonable doubt, as though the documents could compel what they can only invite, and when a thoughtful person noticed the gap between the evidence and the boast, he concluded that the whole thing was a sales pitch. We have also done the reverse. We have turned Easter into a figure of speech about springtime and second chances, which no skeptic needs to refute, because there is nothing in it to be false.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Christians confess that Jesus was raised bodily on the third day, the same Jesus who was buried, and that he was seen. They confess it as something that happened. Paul refused every softer version: "If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied" (1 Corinthians 15:19).

How much weight the historical arguments can bear is a question on which Christians differ. Some think the evidence makes the resurrection highly probable on a historian's own terms. Others think history can only clear the ground, and that faith rests on the testimony of the apostles and the work of the Spirit. This essay does not choose between them.

What the evidence can do is narrow the options. The theft theory explains the tomb and little else. The wrong tomb explains a morning. The legend theory explains how the stories lengthened, but the claim was already there when they were short. The vision theory explains the most, and it strains at a persecutor, a brother and a word. The explanation the witnesses gave covers all of it, and it requires a God who raises the dead. History cannot supply him.

Matthew ends his Gospel on a mountain in Galilee, with the eleven standing in front of the risen Jesus, and he puts a sentence there that an inventor would hardly have wanted: "And when they saw him they worshiped him, but some doubted" (Matthew 28:17). He does not say which of them, or whether it passed. When Paul told the story in Athens some twenty years later, "some mocked," others said, "We will hear you again about this," and a few believed (Acts 17:32–34). The evidence has not changed much since, and neither have the three responses. It has never made the choice for anyone.

*"But these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them."* (Luke 24:11)

*"And when they saw him they worshiped him, but some doubted."* (Matthew 28:17)
